schema.path-missing: `{Path}` is named as a directory of schema files and there is no such directory. Name one that exists, or drop the entry from `Schemas`.
schema.unknown-keyword: `{Written}` starts a line and is not a declaration. A line begins with `struct`, `abstract`, `field`, `enum` or `value`, or it is a comment or blank.
schema.abstract-needs-struct: `abstract` says how the declaration on this line is read, so `struct` has to follow it, and `{Written}` is there instead. Write `abstract struct Reward`.
schema.extends-on-struct-line: `extends` is written on the `struct` line rather than a line of its own - `struct ItemReward extends Reward`. It says which set this struct joins, so it belongs beside the name that joins it.
schema.abstract-cannot-extend: `{Struct}` is `abstract` and extends `{Base}`. A variant cannot itself be abstract: a sheet's `:type` cell names one variant, and a set whose members are themselves sets leaves that cell with more than one answer to what shape the row is.
schema.variant-discriminator-without-bas: `{Struct}` carries `@{Tag}` and extends nothing. That number is a discriminator - which variant of a set this one is - so it only means something on a struct that `extends` an abstract one.
schema.base-unknown: `{Struct}` extends `{Base}` and nothing here declares `{Base}`. The known abstract structs are: {Known}.
schema.base-not-abstract: `{Struct}` extends `{Base}`, and `{Base}` is {What}. Only an `abstract struct` names a set of variants, so that is what `extends` takes.
schema.abstract-without-variants: `abstract struct {Struct}` and nothing extends it. An abstract struct is the name of a set, and a set with no members is a type no column can hold - write `extends {Struct}` on the structs that belong to it, or on the tables that do.
schema.variant-discriminators-collide: `{Struct}` and `{Other}` both extend `{Base}` under `@{Tag}`. The discriminator has to tell them apart, and one number naming two variants means a reader cannot.
schema.variant-discriminators-partial: `{Struct}` extends `{Base}` and carries no discriminator while other variants of `{Base}` do. Number all of them or none: with some numbered, what number an unnumbered variant has depends on how many before it happened to be numbered.
schema.variant-discriminator-reserved: `{Struct}` extends `{Base}` under `@{Tag}`, and `{Other}` holds that number as a tombstone. A dropped variant keeps its number so that nothing else is given it: a reader built while `{Other}` existed still reads `@{Tag}` as that shape, and rows written then still carry it. Give `{Struct}` a number no variant of `{Base}` has ever had.
schema.removed-variant-without-base: `{Struct}` is marked `(removed)` and extends nothing. A tombstone exists to hold a discriminator, and a discriminator only means something inside one set - write `extends` with the abstract struct the dropped variant belonged to, or delete the line.
schema.removed-variant-without-discrimin: `{Struct}` is marked `(removed)`, extends `{Base}` and carries no `@N`. The number is the whole of what a tombstone holds, so without one this line reserves nothing while reading as though it does - write the number the dropped variant had.
schema.abstract-cannot-be-removed: `abstract struct {Struct}` is marked `(removed)`. A tombstone holds one variant's number, and an abstract struct is the set rather than a member of it - there is no number here to keep. Delete the declaration and its variants, or drop the variants one at a time with `(removed)` on each.
schema.abstract-type-not-embeddable: `{Struct}.{Member}` is typed `{Type}`, and `{Type}` is an `abstract struct`. Embedding a variant record in a row is not supported yet. Point at the variants instead - `foreign {Type}` reaches the tables that extend it.
schema.field-outside-struct: `field` with no `struct` above it. A member belongs to the struct declared before it, and there is none in this file yet.
schema.field-in-enum: `field` where the declaration above it is `enum {Enum}`. An enum holds `value` entries; a `field` belongs to a struct.
schema.value-outside-enum: `value` with no `enum` above it. An entry belongs to the enum declared before it, and there is none in this file yet.
schema.value-in-struct: `value` where the declaration above it is `struct {Struct}`. A struct holds `field` members; a `value` belongs to an enum.
schema.name-expected: A declaration needs a name after its keyword, and `{Written}` is where one should be.
schema.name-not-identifier: `{Written}` cannot be a name here. A name starts with a letter or an underscore and carries only letters, digits and underscores, because it becomes a type or a member in every language this tool generates.
schema.type-expected: A member needs a type, and `{Written}` is where one should be. Write a built-in type, a struct or enum declared in these files, or `foreign` and the table a value points at.
schema.foreign-target-expected: `foreign` with no table named after it. Write the table a value is a row of - `foreign Item` - or several separated by `|`.
schema.type-nested-array: An array of arrays. A type carries at most one `[]`: a cell holds a list of values, and a list of lists has no notation in a sheet.
schema.container-arity: `{Type}` takes {Wanted} type argument(s) and was given {Given}.
schema.container-element-meta-outside: `{Struct}.{Member}` is a `{Type}` and carries `{Key}` in its own brackets. A container's element constraints go on the argument they are about - `map<int(min=1),int(max=99)>` - because `map` has two element positions and a key name does not say which one is meant.
schema.container-argument-unsupported: `{Struct}.{Member}` has `{Type}` as a container argument, which is {What}. The file could carry it; the cell notation could not, so the first release leaves it out.
schema.map-key-type-not-allowed: `{Struct}.{Member}` keys a map by `{Type}`. A key has to be a type whose equality is in the value itself: {Allowed}.
schema.set-duplicate-element: `{Table}.{Column}` is a set and this row holds `{Value}` twice - at element {Element}, and already at element {First}. A set states that its elements are distinct, so the second one is either a value nobody meant or the column is a plain array.
schema.map-duplicate-key: `{Table}.{Column}` is a map and this row keys two entries by `{Value}` - element {Element}, and already element {First}. Which of the two a lookup would answer with is not something a file can say.
schema.map-length-mismatch: `{Table}.{Column}` holds {Keys} key(s) and {Values} value(s) in this row - `{Member}`. A map is pairs, so a key with no value beside it has nothing to be a key of.
schema.set-in-a-type-cell: `{Table}.{Column}` is typed `{Type}` in the sheet. A `map` written there becomes two columns and so has a record to publish its lookup on; a `set` is one column and has no such record - the generated code would carry the array and nothing to ask with, which is half a container. Declare the member in a `.tbs` file instead, or type the column `{Element}[]` and let it be a plain array.
schema.container-inside-an-array: `{Table}.{Column}` is a container inside `{Group}`, which the sheet numbered - so it is an array of containers. One column would have to carry a list per element, and a list of lists has no notation in a sheet. Write the group as one record, or make the member a plain array.
schema.container-held-struct-is-a-list: `{Struct}.{Member}` holds `{Type}`, and `{Type}.{Inner}` is `{InnerType}`. Every member of a held struct becomes one column holding every entry's value of it, so a member that is already a list would need a column of lists of lists - which is the same shape `set<T>[]` is refused for.
schema.map-pair-malformed: `{Table}.{Column}` writes its map as pairs and this entry has no `{Separator}` in it - `{Written}`. An entry is a key, the separator, and a value; a value that holds the separator itself writes it `\{Separator}`.
schema.map-pairs-hold-a-struct: `{Table}.{Column}` writes its map as pairs in one cell, and `{Member}` holds `{Type}` - a struct, which is several columns rather than one value. Write the map as a `{Column}.Key` column and a `{Column}.Value` group instead.
schema.map-pairs-table-writes-tags: `{Table}.{Column}` writes its map as pairs in one cell, and `{Table}` writes its own wire tags. A map is two columns, so this one needs two tags and the sheet has written one - write the two columns out, or let the tags be assigned.
schema.map-half-written: `{Table}.{Column}` is a map and has no `{Missing}` column. A map is two columns of equal length, and one of them alone is a list rather than a map.
schema.container-array-not-supported: `{Struct}.{Member}` is `{Type}` - an array whose elements are containers. The file could hold it, and what is missing is a cell notation: an array of sets is a list of lists, and a numbered group of maps has no settled spelling.
schema.type-meta-before-array: Metadata brackets between a type and its `[]`. An array's element constraints go in the declaration's own brackets, told apart from the array's by the key name - `int[] (min=1, size=3)`. Only a container's type arguments carry brackets of their own.
schema.meta-unclosed: Metadata brackets that are never closed. Write `)` at the end of the entries, and quote any value holding a comma.
schema.meta-key-expected: `{Written}` is where a metadata key should be. An entry is a key on its own or `key=value`, and entries are separated by commas.
schema.meta-value-expected: `{Key}=` with nothing after it. Write the value, or drop the `=` to leave the key as a flag.
schema.meta-duplicate-key: `{Key}` is written twice in one set of brackets. Write it once: which of the two applies is not something this can decide.
schema.meta-comment-key: `comment=` is not read here. A description is written as `///` lines above the declaration, which is what lets it run to more than one line and more than one bracket's worth of text.
schema.string-unterminated: A quoted value with no closing quote before the end of the line. A string does not run across lines here; write `\"` for a quote inside one.
schema.block-comment-unterminated: A `/*` with no `*/` after it, so the rest of the file is inside a comment.
schema.wire-tag-not-a-number: `@` needs a whole number after it, and `{Written}` is what is there. A wire tag is what a member's values travel under - `field count@2 int`.
schema.wire-tag-not-positive: A wire tag of {Tag}. Tags count from one.
schema.wire-tag-duplicate: `{Struct}.{Member}` is given tag {Tag}, which `{First}` already carries. Two members under one tag is one member as far as a reader is concerned.
schema.wire-tag-partial: `{Struct}.{Member}` carries no wire tag and other members of the same struct do. Tag all of them or none: with some tagged, what number an untagged member has depends on how many members before it happened to be tagged.
schema.enum-number-duplicate: `{Enum}.{Entry}` is given {Number}, which `{First}` already carries. Two names for one number cannot be told apart in the data.
schema.enum-value-not-a-number: `{Entry}` is given `{Written}`, and an enum entry carries a whole number.
schema.doc-comment-attached-to-nothing: A `///` description with no declaration after it. A description belongs to what it introduces; write the declaration, or make these lines `//` notes.
schema.default-value-expected: `{Member} =` with nothing after it. Write the default value, or drop the `=`.
schema.declared-twice: `{Name}` is declared twice, first at {First}. A name means one thing across every schema file a recipe reads.
schema.name-taken-by-sheet: `{Name}` is declared here and a sheet already declares {What} of that name at {Where}. Two declarations of one name leave nothing to say which a type cell meant; move the sheet's into these files, or rename one of them.
schema.type-unknown: `{Struct}.{Member}` is typed `{Type}`, which is neither a built-in type nor anything declared in these files.
schema.type-is-sheet-enum: `{Struct}.{Member}` is typed `{Type}`, which a sheet declares. A member's type has to be found in these files alone, so that an editor can read them without opening a workbook - move the enum here, or type the member with the integer it carries.
schema.container-not-supported: `{Struct}.{Member}` is typed `{Type}`. The notation reads it and this build does not carry it yet; the file format needs no change for it, so what is missing is the container in each generated language.
schema.struct-cycle: `{Cycle}` holds itself. A struct is spread across columns, so a struct that contains itself has no end - a relationship that loops is written as a reference, which is what `foreign` is for.
schema.enum-number-out-of-range: `{Enum}.{Entry}` is given {Number}, and an enum entry carries a 32-bit number.
schema.group-typed-twice: `{Table}.{Group}` is typed `{First}` by one of its columns and `{Second}` by another. One column of a group names the struct and the rest leave their type cells empty; two of them naming one leaves nothing to say which the group is.
schema.column-not-a-member: `{Table}.{Column}` is in a group typed `{Struct}`, and `{Struct}` has no member of that name. Add the member to the declaration, or take the column out of the group.
schema.column-type-disagrees: `{Table}.{Column}` is typed `{Written}` and `{Struct}.{Member}` is declared `{Declared}`. Empty the type cell to take the declaration's, or make the two agree.
schema.member-type-unusable: `{Struct}.{Member}` is declared `{Declared}`, which one column cannot hold. A member that is a struct is written as a column per its own members; an array of references is not carried at all.
schema.member-has-no-column: `{Table}.{Group}` is typed `{Struct}` and has no column for its member `{Member}`. A type says what a value of it holds, so a group missing one of its members is not that type - write the column, or take the member out of the declaration.
schema.column-has-no-type: `{Table}.{Column}` has an empty type cell and is in no group that names a struct. A type cell may be left empty only where a declaration fills it in.
schema.column-typed-with-a-struct: `{Table}.{Column}` is typed `{Written}`, which is a declared struct, and the column is not part of a group. A struct types a group of columns - `{Written}1.Member` - and writing one whole value into a single cell is a notation this build does not carry yet.
schema.meta-key-unknown: `{Key}` on `{Where}` is not a key anything reads. Nothing here checks a key's spelling as it is written, so a key nobody claims is reported once every declaration is in - which is what stops a misspelt one from quietly saying nothing. A key of your own goes under `x.`, which is never reported.
schema.meta-key-not-carried: `{Key}` on `{Where}` is a key this notation defines and this build does not act on yet. Ignoring it would leave you believing it applies; take it out until it is carried.
schema.meta-refs-is-foreign: `{Key}` on `{Where}` is a check, and this column is already a reference. `foreign` names one table and resolves it, which says more than `refs` does - drop one of the two.
schema.role-not-a-string: `{Key}` on `{Member}` says what a string is for, and the member is declared `{Type}`.
schema.role-written-twice: `{Member}` is marked both `text` and `asset`. A string has one thing it is for.
schema.role-space-without-text: `{Member}` names a `namespace` and is neither `text` nor `asset`. A namespace qualifies the set a `text` column is gathered into, so there is nothing here for it to qualify.
schema.role-space-not-text: `{Member}` names a `namespace` and is an `asset`. A namespace is a `text` thing - the folders an asset is looked for in come from the recipe, keyed by the kind.
schema.bound-not-a-number: `{Key}` on `{Member}` is `{Written}`, and a bound is a number.
schema.allowed-empty: `allowed` on `{Member}` lists no values. Write them separated by `;`, or drop the key.
schema.allowed-intersection-empty: `{Table}.{Column}` allows `{Sheet}` and `{Member}` is declared to allow `{Declared}`, and the two have nothing in common. A value must satisfy both, so this column can hold nothing at all.
schema.refs-empty: `refs` on `{Member}` names no table. Write them separated by `;`, or drop the key.
schema.refs-intersection-empty: `{Table}.{Column}` checks against `{Sheet}` and `{Member}` is declared to check against `{Declared}`, and the two have nothing in common. A value must satisfy both, so this column can hold nothing at all.
schema.sep-not-one-character: `sep` on `{Struct}` is `{Written}`, and a separator is one character.
schema.sep-member-not-scalar: `{Struct}.{Member}` is `{Type}`, and `{Struct}` writes a whole value into one cell. One component is one value, so a member that is itself several - a record, an array - has no place in the cell to be written. Take `sep` off the struct, or write this member's own columns instead.
schema.sep-column-is-an-index: `{Table}.{Column}` is `{Struct}`, which holds several values in one cell, and the column identifies the row. A key is one value: index the table by one of the members instead.
schema.sep-table-writes-tags: `{Table}` writes its wire tags out with `@N`, and `{Column}` is `{Struct}` - which becomes one column per member and so needs a tag for each. Write the members as their own columns, each with its own tag.
schema.sep-column-has-constraints: `{Table}.{Column}` is `{Struct}` and declares a column constraint. What a bound means for a value with several members is not decided, so it is refused rather than read one of the ways. Declare the bound on the member instead.
schema.sep-component-count: `{Table}.{Column}` holds {Given} value(s) and `{Struct}` has {Wanted} member(s). A cell is read by position, so the count has to match exactly - written: `{Written}`.
schema.default-and-optional: `{Struct}.{Member}` is `{Type}` and is given the default `{Written}`, which says two things about one blank cell: that a row may leave the value out, and that leaving it out means `{Written}`. The second answer makes the first unreachable. Drop the `?`, or drop the default.
schema.default-unreadable: `{Member}` is given the default `{Written}`, which `{Type}` cannot read: {Detail}
schema.default-on-an-index: `{Table}.{Column}` identifies the row and `{Struct}.{Member}` declares the default `{Written}`. Every row leaving the cell blank would take that same key, which is what an absent index is refused for.
schema.default-needs-an-empty-type-cell: `{Table}.{Column}` writes the type `{Written}` and `{Struct}.{Member}` declares a default. A written type is read while the sheet is being parsed, which settles what a blank cell means before the declaration is consulted - so a member with a default needs its column's type cell left empty for the declaration to fill in.
schema.pattern-written-twice: `{Table}.{Column}` declares the pattern `{Sheet}` and `{Member}` declares `{Declared}`. Two bounds have a tighter one and two whitelists have what they share, but two patterns have neither - so which of these applies is not something this can decide. Write one of them.
schema.size-not-a-count: `size` on `{Member}` is `{Written}`, and a length is a whole number or a range of them - `4`, `1..3`, `2..`.
schema.pattern-not-a-string: `regex` on `{Member}` is a pattern for text, and the member is declared `{Type}`. Matching against a formatted number is not what a pattern here would mean.
schema.size-not-an-array: `size` on `{Member}` is how many elements a cell holds, and the member is declared `{Type}`. A value that is not an array holds one by being one.
schema.abstract-type-on-a-member-column: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` is typed `{Struct}`, which is an abstract type. An abstract type has no fixed field list, so it cannot be the type of a member - it is the type of the group, and the group states it on its `$type` column. Write `{Group}.$type` and put `{Struct}` in that column's type cell.
schema.member-no-variant-declares: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` is not a member of `{Struct}` nor of any of its variants. The columns of a polymorphic group are the union of the variants' members, so a name none of them declares has nothing to read it. Variants: `{Variants}`.
schema.member-type-varies-by-variant: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` is declared `{FirstType}` by `{First}` and `{SecondType}` by `{Second}`, both variants of `{Struct}`. Variants sharing a member name share one column, and one column carries one type - give the two members different names, or give them the same type.
schema.discriminator-cell-blank: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` is blank on a row. It carries which variant of `{Struct}` that row is, and nothing else in the group can be read without it - which member columns apply is exactly what this cell answers. Write one of `{Variants}`.
schema.discriminator-cell-unknown: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` holds `{Written}`, which is not a variant of `{Struct}`. Variants: `{Variants}`.
schema.value-outside-the-rows-variant: Column `{Column}` of `{Table}` holds a value on a row whose variant is `{Variant}`, and that column belongs to `{Declared}`. The columns of a polymorphic group are every variant's members side by side, so a row always has blank cells that are not its own - and nothing would read this one, because the generated `{Variant}` has no such member.
